knowledge_refs.formula_empty_justification: The only relationship used is basic right-triangle trigonometry to resolve components; it is not a major reusable syllabus physics formula.

hints: Draw the 12 m s⁻¹ velocity as the hypotenuse of a right-angled component triangle.
The stated 50° is measured from the horizontal, so the horizontal component is adjacent to that angle.
walkthrough: The initial speed is 12 m s⁻¹ at 50° above the horizontal.
In the component triangle, the horizontal component is adjacent to the 50° angle.
Use horizontal component = 12 cos 50°.
Calculate 12 cos 50° = 7.713... m s⁻¹.
To two significant figures, the horizontal component is 7.7 m s⁻¹.

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves the 12 m s⁻¹ velocity horizontally using cos 50° and obtains 7.7 m s⁻¹.

knowledge_refs.formula_empty_justification: The only relationships used are basic right-triangle trigonometry or the component ratio; neither is a major reusable syllabus physics formula.

hints: The vertical component is perpendicular to the horizontal component in the same velocity triangle.
Because 50° is measured from the horizontal, the vertical component is opposite the angle.
walkthrough: The initial velocity has magnitude 12 m s⁻¹ and is 50° above the horizontal.
The vertical component is opposite the 50° angle in the component triangle.
Use vertical component = 12 sin 50°.
Calculate 12 sin 50° = 9.192... m s⁻¹.
To two significant figures, the vertical component is 9.2 m s⁻¹.
Equivalently, using the horizontal component from (a)(i), 7.7 tan 50° also gives about 9.2 m s⁻¹.

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves the 12 m s⁻¹ velocity vertically using 12 sin 50°, or an equivalent component route, and obtains 9.2 m s⁻¹.

hints: Consider the vertical motion only, using the vertical launch component from part (a)(ii).
At maximum height, the vertical velocity is zero; use v² = u² + 2as with upward as positive.
walkthrough: The initial vertical velocity is u = 9.2 m s⁻¹ from part (a)(ii).
At maximum height the vertical velocity is v = 0, and taking upward as positive gives a = −9.81 m s⁻².
Rearrange: 2(9.81)h = 9.2².
Therefore the maximum height reached is 4.3 m.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses a valid vertical-motion relationship with the vertical velocity zero at maximum height, or an equivalent accepted energy or time route.
Obtains a maximum height of 4.3 m, or an equivalent unrounded value.

hints: The ball reaches Q when its vertical velocity falls from 9.2 m s⁻¹ to zero under gravitational acceleration.
Use that time with the unchanged horizontal velocity to find the horizontal separation from P to Q.
The horizontal separation and the 4.3 m height are perpendicular components of displacement PQ.
walkthrough: At Q, the vertical velocity is zero. Take upward as positive and use v = u + at: 0 = 9.2 − 9.81t.
The time to Q is t = 9.2 / 9.81 = 0.938... s.
Air resistance is negligible, so the horizontal velocity remains 7.7 m s⁻¹.
The horizontal separation is x = vt = 7.7 × 0.938... = 7.23 m.
The vertical separation from P to Q is the maximum height 4.3 m found in part (b).
These separations are perpendicular, so |PQ| = √(7.23² + 4.3²).
Calculate |PQ| = 8.41... m.
Therefore the magnitude of displacement PQ is 8.4 m.

ai_rubric.observable: Uses the vertical component and gravitational acceleration to determine a time to Q of about 0.94 s.
Uses the constant horizontal component and the flight time to obtain a horizontal separation of about 7.23 m.
Combines the perpendicular horizontal and vertical separations using a right-triangle magnitude calculation.
Obtains a displacement magnitude of 8.4 m.
